claim: Eleven participants (7 males, 14–45 y of age) were implanted subdurally with grid and strip electrode arrays on the cortical surface to localize the seizure onset zone for subsequent surgical resection.
source: Eleven participants (7 males, 14–45 y of age) were implanted subdurally with grid and strip electrode arrays on the cortical surface to localize the seizure onset zone for subsequent surgical resection (Figure 1A).
evidence: Direct statement about participant demographics and surgical procedure in the Methods section.

claim: Eight participants had electrode arrays placed on the left hemisphere.
source: The electrode arrays (10 mm inter-electrode spacing, 2.3 mm exposed diameter; Ad-Tech, Racine, USA) were placed at the University Medical Center Utrecht, The Netherlands, on either right or left (eight cases) hemisphere.
evidence: Direct statement about electrode placement in the Methods section.

claim: The electrode arrays had 10 mm inter-electrode spacing and 2.3 mm exposed diameter.
source: The electrode arrays (10 mm inter-electrode spacing, 2.3 mm exposed diameter; Ad-Tech, Racine, USA) were placed at the University Medical Center Utrecht, The Netherlands, on either right or left (eight cases) hemisphere.
evidence: Direct specification of electrode technical parameters.

claim: The mean number of electrodes per participant was 81.3 ± 11.2.
source: The number and anatomical location of the electrodes varied across participants, depending on the clinical considerations specific to each case (mean number of electrodes ± SEM: 81.3 ± 11.2).
evidence: Direct statement of measured electrode count with statistical measure.

claim: Two participants had difficulties adhering to the task instructions and frequently confused left- and right-hand conditions.
source: Two participants had difficulties adhering to the task instructions and frequently confused left- and right-hand conditions of the study.
evidence: Direct observation of participant behavior during the study.

claim: One participant had cavernous malformations in temporoparietal and frontal cortex.
source: One of these participants had cavernous malformations in temporoparietal and frontal cortex.
evidence: Direct statement about participant's clinical condition.

claim: Nine participants were included in the analysis of behavioral data.
source: The other participant had experienced medical complications prior to task performance, leaving nine participants for analysis of the behavioral data.
evidence: Direct statement about final sample size for behavioral analysis.

claim: Seven participants were included in the analysis of neural data.
source: Two participants had no electrode coverage of upper-limb sensorimotor areas as indicated by electrocortical stimulation, leaving seven participants for analysis of the neural data.
evidence: Direct statement about final sample size for neural analysis.

claim: Participants performed up to three sessions of the movement imagery task.
source: Participants were positioned in a semi-recumbent position in their hospital bed and performed up to three sessions of a movement imagery task (mean number of sessions ± SEM: 2 ± 0.2).
evidence: Direct statement about task administration.

claim: The mean number of sessions performed was 2 ± 0.2.
source: Participants were positioned in a semi-recumbent position in their hospital bed and performed up to three sessions of a movement imagery task (mean number of sessions ± SEM: 2 ± 0.2).
evidence: Direct statement of measured session count with statistical measure.

claim: The cylinder was tilted according to 1 of 15 possible orientations, 24° apart.
source: The cylinder, tilted according to 1 of 15 possible orientations (24° apart, presented pseudo-randomly, size 17.5 × 3.5 cm), was presented on a gray background at the center of the computer screen that was placed within reaching distance in front of the participant.
evidence: Direct specification of experimental stimulus parameters.

claim: The cylinder size was 17.5 × 3.5 cm.
source: The cylinder, tilted according to 1 of 15 possible orientations (24° apart, presented pseudo-randomly, size 17.5 × 3.5 cm), was presented on a gray background at the center of the computer screen that was placed within reaching distance in front of the participant.
evidence: Direct specification of stimulus dimensions.

claim: The duration for which the cylinder stayed on the screen was adjusted for each participant (2–5 s).
source: The duration for which the cylinder stayed on the screen was adjusted for each participant (2–5 s) such that they could comfortably perform the task at a pace that suited their current physical and mental state.
evidence: Direct statement about individualized timing parameters.

claim: A single session consisted of 60 trials (10 min).
source: A single session consisted of 60 trials (10 min).
evidence: Direct specification of session structure.

claim: The hand used to imagine the movement alternated every ten trials.
source: The hand used to imagine the movement alternated every ten trials, prompted by a visual cue.
evidence: Direct description of experimental design.

claim: A sine-wave fit to the over-/underhand data points explained 81 ± 4% of the variance in the left-hand condition (t(8) = 18.4, p<0.001).
source: This is supported by a psychophysical analysis showing that a sine-wave fit to the over-/underhand data points explained 81 ± 4% of the variance in the left-hand condition (M ± SEM; t(8) = 18.4, p<0.001) and 76 ± 4% in the right-hand condition (t(8) = 21.6, p<0.001), consistent with the prediction of two orientation-dependent switch points in each hand's response curve, that is the 50% crossings in Figure 1C (Brinkman et al., 2014).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data with reported test statistics.

claim: A sine-wave fit to the over-/underhand data points explained 76 ± 4% of the variance in the right-hand condition (t(8) = 21.6, p<0.001).
source: This is supported by a psychophysical analysis showing that a sine-wave fit to the over-/underhand data points explained 81 ± 4% of the variance in the left-hand condition (M ± SEM; t(8) = 18.4, p<0.001) and 76 ± 4% in the right-hand condition (t(8) = 21.6, p<0.001), consistent with the prediction of two orientation-dependent switch points in each hand's response curve, that is the 50% crossings in Figure 1C (Brinkman et al., 2014).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data with reported test statistics.

claim: Eight out of nine participants completed a control task.
source: Eight out of nine participants additionally completed a control task that used the same visual input and response contingencies as the motor imagery task, but where no imagery was required.
evidence: Direct statement about control task participation.

claim: Participants performed the control task with 99.4 ± 0.3% accuracy.
source: Participants performed the control task with high accuracy (99.4 ± 0.3% correct, M ± SEM).
evidence: Direct measurement of task performance with statistical measure.

claim: All 20 electrodes with alpha-band local maxima were located posterior to the central sulcus (χ2(19)=40, p<0.001).
source: All 20 electrodes with alpha-band local maxima were located posterior to the central sulcus, χ2(19)=40, p<0.001 (pre vs. postcentral sulcus), see the red electrodes in Figure 2D.
evidence: Statistical analysis of electrode locations with chi-squared test.

claim: The 17 electrodes with beta-band local maxima were localized to both sides of the central sulcus (χ2(16)=1.1, p=0.3).
source: As seen in the same figure, the 17 blue electrodes with beta-band local maxima were localized to both sides of the central sulcus, χ2(16)=1.1, p=0.3 (7 pre- and 10 postcentral).
evidence: Statistical analysis of electrode locations with chi-squared test.

claim: Seven out of 17 beta-band local maxima electrodes were precentral and 10 were postcentral.
source: As seen in the same figure, the 17 blue electrodes with beta-band local maxima were localized to both sides of the central sulcus, χ2(16)=1.1, p=0.3 (7 pre- and 10 postcentral).
evidence: Direct count of electrode locations.

claim: Only 7 out of 30 combined unique electrodes were local maxima for both sensorimotor rhythms (χ2(29)=17, p<0.001).
source: Furthermore, only 7 out of 30 combined unique electrodes were local maxima for both sensorimotor rhythms, suggesting that alpha- and beta-band rhythms involve largely different neuronal ensembles, χ2(29)=17, p<0.001.
evidence: Statistical analysis of electrode overlap with chi-squared test.

claim: Alpha- and beta-band local maxima were separated by an average of 11.8 ± 2.2 mm.
source: On average, alpha- and beta-band local maxima were separated by 11.8 ± 2.2 mm (M ± SEM).
evidence: Direct measurement of spatial separation with statistical measure.

claim: Alpha electrodes yielded predominantly (14 out of 20 electrodes, 70%) somatosensory sensations of the contralateral upper limb following electrical stimulation (χ2(19)=12.4, p<0.001).
source: As indicated in Figure 2D, alpha electrodes yielded predominantly (14 out of 20 electrodes, 70%) somatosensory sensations of the contralateral upper limb following electrical stimulation, χ2(19)=12.4, p<0.001.
evidence: Statistical analysis of stimulation responses with chi-squared test.

claim: Three out of 20 alpha electrodes (15%) were part of stimulation electrode pairs yielding both somatomotor and somatosensory responses.
source: Additionally, a subset of electrodes (3 out of 20, 15%) were part of equally many stimulation electrode pairs yielding both somatomotor and somatosensory responses.
evidence: Direct count of electrode response types.

claim: Beta electrodes were marginally more likely (11 out of 17, 65%) to elicit a somatomotor than a somatosensory response following electrical stimulation (χ2(16)=2.9, p=0.086).
source: By contrast, beta electrodes were marginally more likely (11 out of 17, 65%) to elicit a somatomotor than a somatosensory response of the upper limb following electrical stimulation, χ2(16)=2.9, p=0.086.
evidence: Statistical analysis of stimulation responses with chi-squared test.

claim: The temporal dynamics of alpha and beta power were highly correlated (r = 0.7 ± 0.1, p<0.002).
source: These temporal dynamics were highly correlated (r = 0.7 ± 0.1, M ± SEM, p<0.002) and both alpha- and beta-band power was more strongly attenuated for the hemisphere contralateral to the arm used in the imagined movement, see Figure 2E.
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis with reported correlation coefficient and p-value.

claim: Alpha-band power increased by 34% in the ipsilateral cortex between 910 and 1220 ms (p<0.05).
source: Yet it can be seen from the same graph that alpha-band power increases in the (postcentral) cortex ipsilateral to the arm used for imagery, as compared to baseline levels (+34% between 910 and 1220 ms, p<0.05; alpha-band power also decreased by 26% and 32% in the contralateral cortex between 170 and 850 ms and between 1230 and 2000 ms, respectively).
evidence: Statistical analysis of power changes with reported percentage and p-value.

claim: Alpha-band power decreased by 26% in the contralateral cortex between 170 and 850 ms.
source: Yet it can be seen from the same graph that alpha-band power increases in the (postcentral) cortex ipsilateral to the arm used for imagery, as compared to baseline levels (+34% between 910 and 1220 ms, p<0.05; alpha-band power also decreased by 26% and 32% in the contralateral cortex between 170 and 850 ms and between 1230 and 2000 ms, respectively).
evidence: Statistical analysis of power changes with reported percentage.

claim: Alpha-band power decreased by 32% in the contralateral cortex between 1230 and 2000 ms.
source: Yet it can be seen from the same graph that alpha-band power increases in the (postcentral) cortex ipsilateral to the arm used for imagery, as compared to baseline levels (+34% between 910 and 1220 ms, p<0.05; alpha-band power also decreased by 26% and 32% in the contralateral cortex between 170 and 850 ms and between 1230 and 2000 ms, respectively).
evidence: Statistical analysis of power changes with reported percentage.

claim: Beta-band power decreased by 21% in the contralateral cortex between 150 and 760 ms.
source: In contrast, beta-band power decreases further in the (pre- and postcentral) contralateral cortex (−21% between 150 and 760 ms vs. −13% in the ipsilateral cortex between −180 and 580 ms; there was another statistically significant change of −21% from baseline in the contralateral cortex between 1450 and 2000 ms).
evidence: Statistical analysis of power changes with reported percentage.

claim: Beta-band power decreased by 13% in the ipsilateral cortex between −180 and 580 ms.
source: In contrast, beta-band power decreases further in the (pre- and postcentral) contralateral cortex (−21% between 150 and 760 ms vs. −13% in the ipsilateral cortex between −180 and 580 ms; there was another statistically significant change of −21% from baseline in the contralateral cortex between 1450 and 2000 ms).
evidence: Statistical analysis of power changes with reported percentage.

claim: Beta-band power decreased by 21% in the contralateral cortex between 1450 and 2000 ms.
source: In contrast, beta-band power decreases further in the (pre- and postcentral) contralateral cortex (−21% between 150 and 760 ms vs. −13% in the ipsilateral cortex between −180 and 580 ms; there was another statistically significant change of −21% from baseline in the contralateral cortex between 1450 and 2000 ms).
evidence: Statistical analysis of power changes with reported percentage.

claim: Alpha- and beta-band rhythms were temporally and spatially uncorrelated (all BF01 >1.56 in favor of the null hypothesis).
source: It can be seen from the leftmost bars in these figures that alpha- and beta-band rhythms were temporally as well as spatially uncorrelated (all BF01 >1.56 in favor of the null hypothesis of no correlation).
evidence: Bayesian statistical analysis with reported Bayes Factors.

claim: Alpha- and beta-band rhythms showed weak resemblances in sensitivity to trial-by-trial demands (BF01s of 1.06, 1.01, and 0.73).
source: Alpha- and beta-band rhythms showed weak resemblances in sensitivity to trial-by-trial demands, for both sensorimotor demands contained by temporal dynamics and activity patterns (Figure 3D–F, BF01s of 1.06, 1.01, and 0.73, respectively).
evidence: Bayesian statistical analysis with reported Bayes Factors.

claim: High-frequency activity showed spatial and temporal correspondences with both alpha- and beta-band rhythmic activity during movement imagery.
source: High-frequency activity showed spatial and temporal correspondences with both alpha- and beta-band rhythmic activity during movement imagery (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Direct statement about observed correlations with reference to figures.

claim: Local maxima in high-frequency activity involved 14 out of 22 electrodes: four producing alpha, four producing beta, six producing both alpha and beta, and eight with no overlap.
source: This is also seen in the spatial distribution of local maxima in high-frequency activity (green electrodes in Figure 2D), which were localized to both sides of the central sulcus and involved neuronal ensembles producing alpha- or beta-band rhythmic activity (14/22: four producing alpha, four producing beta, six producing both alpha and beta, and eight with no overlap).
evidence: Direct count of electrode overlap patterns.

claim: Only 3 out of 47 combined unique electrodes were both local maxima for high-frequency activity and local inhibition as indexed by the 1/f slope.
source: The spatial specificity of the 1/f slope index is further supported by a direct comparison with the spatial distribution of high-frequency activity: despite superficially similar distributions across the central sulcus (Figure 2D), only 3 out of 47 combined unique electrodes were both local maxima for high-frequency activity and local inhibition as indexed by the 1/f slope.
evidence: Direct count of electrode overlap.

claim: Electrodes with local maxima in beta-band activity and local inhibition had 59% (10/17) spatial correspondence.
source: Furthermore, electrodes with local maxima in beta-band activity and local inhibition were similarly distributed across the central sulcus, with a 59% (10/17) spatial correspondence.
evidence: Direct calculation of spatial overlap percentage.

claim: There was a 25% correspondence (5/20) between electrodes with local maxima in alpha-band activity and local inhibition.
source: In contrast, the 1/f slope index had a different relationship with alpha-band responses to task demands. The putative index of excitation/inhibition balance was not spatially related to the alpha-band response (Figure 3B,C), with a 25% correspondence (5/20) between electrodes with local maxima in alpha-band activity and local inhibition.
evidence: Direct calculation of spatial overlap percentage.

claim: There was a significant temporal anti-correlation between local maxima of alpha-band power and 1/f slope.
source: However, there was a significant temporal anti-correlation between local maxima of alpha-band power and 1/f slope (Figure 3A).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis with reference to figure.

claim: Both alpha and beta phase gradients exhibited a higher degree of alignment across sensorimotor cortex than expected by chance (mean alpha PGD = 0.37, mean beta PGD = 0.35, p<0.001 in each patient).
source: As seen through the small cone-shaped arrows positioned over each corresponding grid-electrode in Figure 4A, both alpha and beta phase gradients exhibited a higher degree of alignment across sensorimotor cortex than expected by chance (mean alpha PGD = 0.37, mean beta PGD = 0.35, p<0.001 in each patient for both alpha and beta, estimated from shuffled data).
evidence: Statistical analysis of phase gradient directionality with reported values and p-values.

claim: The traveling waves moved in a consistent direction across trials and over trial-time (Rayleigh test of uniformity, p<10−18 in 5 out of 6 patients for alpha, p<10−91 in each patient for beta).
source: The traveling waves moved in a consistent direction across trials and over trial-time (circular histograms in Figure 4A; Rayleigh test of uniformity, p<10−18 in 5 out of 6 patients for alpha, p<10−91 in each patient for beta).
evidence: Statistical analysis using Rayleigh test with reported p-values.

claim: Mean propagation speeds of the sensorimotor waves ranged between 5 and 9 cm/s for alpha and between 11 and 21 cm/s for beta.
source: Across participants, mean propagation speeds of the sensorimotor waves ranged between 5 and 9 cm/s for alpha and between 11 and 21 cm/s for beta (Figure 4B), consistent with previous reports of traveling beta waves in motor cortex (Rubino et al., 2006) and in the lower range of traveling alpha waves observed in posterior cortex (Bahramisharif et al., 2013; Halgren et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: Direct measurement of wave propagation speeds with reference to figure and citations.

claim: Alpha waves propagated in a caudo-rostral direction, while beta waves advanced in a rostro-caudal direction.
source: Alpha waves propagated in a caudo-rostral direction, while beta waves advanced in a rostro-caudal direction (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct observation of wave propagation directions with reference to figures.

claim: The distribution of propagation directions in individual participants showed that alpha and beta traveling waves propagate independently (mean Kullback-Leibler divergence = 0.10, p<0.001 in each patient).
source: A novel finding of this study is that alpha and beta traveling waves propagate independently across sensorimotor cortex, as indicated by the distribution of propagation directions in individual participants (Figure 4A, Videos 1 and 2) and by the mean probability distribution over participants (Figure 4C; mean Kullback-Leibler divergence = 0.10, p<0.001 in each patient, estimated from shuffled data).
evidence: Statistical analysis using Kullback-Leibler divergence with reported values and p-values.

claim: Alpha rhythms propagated in a more consistent direction during imagined movement of the ipsilateral arm.
source: As seen in Figure 4D, alpha rhythms propagated in a more consistent direction during imagined movement of the ipsilateral arm, while the propagation direction of beta rhythms became more consistent during imagined movement of the contralateral arm, as compared to baseline levels (see Figure 4—figure supplement 2 for the effects of task demand).
evidence: Direct observation of directional consistency changes with reference to figures.

claim: Beta rhythms propagated in a more consistent direction during imagined movement of the contralateral arm.
source: As seen in Figure 4D, alpha rhythms propagated in a more consistent direction during imagined movement of the ipsilateral arm, while the propagation direction of beta rhythms became more consistent during imagined movement of the contralateral arm, as compared to baseline levels (see Figure 4—figure supplement 2 for the effects of task demand).
evidence: Direct observation of directional consistency changes with reference to figures.

claim: On average, alpha and beta rhythmic activity were centered on 7.4 ± 0.7 and 16.9 ± 1.1 Hz, respectively.
source: This adaptive approach (Source code 1) avoids having to rely on canonical frequency bands that due in part to their narrowness may not accurately capture the neural phenomena of interest in each individual (Haegens et al., 2014; Szurhaj et al., 2003). On average, alpha and beta rhythmic activity were centered on 7.4 ± 0.7 and 16.9 ± 1.1 Hz, respectively.
evidence: Direct measurement of frequency centers with statistical measures and citations.

claim: Five out of seven participants had a rhythmic power-spectral component that overlapped with the 8–12 Hz alpha frequency range.
source: Five out of seven participants had a rhythmic power-spectral component that overlapped with the 8–12 Hz alpha frequency range, one had a rhythmic component below that range, and all seven had a rhythmic component that overlapped with the 15–25 Hz beta range (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct count of participants with specific spectral features.

claim: One participant had a rhythmic component below the 8–12 Hz alpha frequency range.
source: Five out of seven participants had a rhythmic power-spectral component that overlapped with the 8–12 Hz alpha frequency range, one had a rhythmic component below that range, and all seven had a rhythmic component that overlapped with the 15–25 Hz beta range (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct count of participants with specific spectral features.

claim: All seven participants had a rhythmic component that overlapped with the 15–25 Hz beta range.
source: Five out of seven participants had a rhythmic power-spectral component that overlapped with the 8–12 Hz alpha frequency range, one had a rhythmic component below that range, and all seven had a rhythmic component that overlapped with the 15–25 Hz beta range (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct count of participants with specific spectral features.

claim: Participant S7 exhibited only a single rhythmic component (in the beta frequency range) and was excluded from further analysis.
source: Participant S7 exhibited only a single rhythmic component (in the beta frequency range) and was excluded from further analysis.
evidence: Direct statement about participant exclusion criterion.

claim: The analysis yielded 4.0 ± 1.2 alpha and 3.4 ± 0.8 beta peak activity electrodes for participants S1 - S5.
source: This analysis yielded 4.0 ± 1.2 alpha and 3.4 ± 0.8 beta peak activity electrodes for participants S1 - S5 (M ± SEM, red and blue electrodes in Figures 2A and 1).
evidence: Direct count of identified electrodes with statistical measures.

claim: Electrophysiological data were acquired using the 128-channel Micromed recording system, analog-filtered between 0.15 and 134.4 Hz, and digitally sampled at 512 Hz.
source: Electrophysiological data were acquired using the 128-channel Micromed recording system (Treviso, Italy, 22 bits), analog-filtered between 0.15 and 134.4 Hz, and digitally sampled at 512 Hz.
evidence: Direct specification of data acquisition parameters.

claim: Epochs where overt movements or distracting events occurred were excluded from the analysis (6 ± 2% of the total amount of trials).
source: During the recordings, participants were closely monitored for overt movements or distracting events. Epochs were these occurred were excluded from the analysis (6 ± 2% of the total amount of trials).
evidence: Direct statement of data exclusion criteria with percentage.

claim: Data with epileptic activity or other artifacts were excluded (2 ± 2% of the total amount of trials).
source: The electrophysiological signals were visually inspected to ensure that they were free of epileptic activity or other artifacts (2 ± 2% of the total amount of trials excluded).
evidence: Direct statement of data exclusion criteria with percentage.

claim: Both alpha- and beta-band rhythms displayed effector-specific modulations.
source: Both rhythms displayed effector-specific modulations, tracked spectral markers of action potentials in the local neuronal population, and showed spatially systematic phase relationships (traveling waves).
evidence: Direct statement in the Abstract summarizing findings.

claim: Both alpha- and beta-band rhythms tracked spectral markers of action potentials in the local neuronal population.
source: Both rhythms displayed effector-specific modulations, tracked spectral markers of action potentials in the local neuronal population, and showed spatially systematic phase relationships (traveling waves).
evidence: Direct statement in the Abstract summarizing findings.

claim: Both alpha- and beta-band rhythms showed spatially systematic phase relationships (traveling waves).
source: Both rhythms displayed effector-specific modulations, tracked spectral markers of action potentials in the local neuronal population, and showed spatially systematic phase relationships (traveling waves).
evidence: Direct statement in the Abstract summarizing findings.

claim: Alpha- and beta-band rhythms differed in their anatomical and functional properties.
source: Yet, alpha- and beta-band rhythms differed in their anatomical and functional properties, were weakly correlated, and traveled along opposite directions across the sensorimotor cortex.
evidence: Direct statement in the Abstract summarizing findings.

claim: Alpha- and beta-band rhythms were weakly correlated.
source: Yet, alpha- and beta-band rhythms differed in their anatomical and functional properties, were weakly correlated, and traveled along opposite directions across the sensorimotor cortex.
evidence: Direct statement in the Abstract summarizing findings.

claim: Alpha- and beta-band rhythms traveled along opposite directions across the sensorimotor cortex.
source: Yet, alpha- and beta-band rhythms differed in their anatomical and functional properties, were weakly correlated, and traveled along opposite directions across the sensorimotor cortex.
evidence: Direct statement in the Abstract summarizing findings.

claim: Increased alpha-band power in the somatosensory cortex ipsilateral to the selected arm was associated with spatially-unspecific inhibition.
source: Increased alpha-band power in the somatosensory cortex ipsilateral to the selected arm was associated with spatially-unspecific inhibition.
evidence: Direct statement in the Abstract summarizing findings.

claim: Decreased beta-band power over contralateral motor cortex was associated with a focal shift from relative inhibition to excitation.
source: Decreased beta-band power over contralateral motor cortex was associated with a focal shift from relative inhibition to excitation.
evidence: Direct statement in the Abstract summarizing findings.

claim: Movement selection and motor imagery evoke the same activity patterns in dorsal premotor cortex and in the subthalamic nucleus.
source: Besides sharing motor control variables and sensitivity to biomechanical constraints (de Lange et al., 2006; Gentili et al., 2004; Vargas et al., 2004), movement selection and motor imagery evoke the same activity patterns in dorsal premotor cortex and in the subthalamic nucleus (Cisek and Kalaska, 2004; Kühn et al., 2006), leading to similar consequences on the excitability of the corticospinal system (Lebon et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Movement selection and motor imagery lead to similar consequences on the excitability of the corticospinal system.
source: Besides sharing motor control variables and sensitivity to biomechanical constraints (de Lange et al., 2006; Gentili et al., 2004; Vargas et al., 2004), movement selection and motor imagery evoke the same activity patterns in dorsal premotor cortex and in the subthalamic nucleus (Cisek and Kalaska, 2004; Kühn et al., 2006), leading to similar consequences on the excitability of the corticospinal system (Lebon et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior research.

claim: High-frequency (60–120 Hz) content in the ECoG signal is a mesoscale correlate of action potentials and dendritic currents in the local neural population.
source: First, we considered high-frequency (60–120 Hz) content in the ECoG signal, a mesoscale correlate of action potentials and dendritic currents in the local neural population (Leszczynski et al., 2019; Manning et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2009; Ray and Maunsell, 2011; Rich and Wallis, 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The slope of the power-spectral density function (1/f slope) is a putative summary index of synaptic excitation/inhibition balance.
source: Second, we considered the slope of the power-spectral density function (1/f slope), a putative summary index of synaptic excitation/inhibition balance (Gao et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior research.

claim: There are differences in the cortico-subcortical loops supporting alpha- and beta-band rhythms.
source: For instance, there are differences in the cortico-subcortical loops supporting alpha- and beta-band rhythms (Bastos et al., 2014; Leventhal et al., 2012; Schreckenberger et al., 2004; West et al., 2018), and only the latter rhythm has clear modulatory effects on corticospinal neurons (Baker et al., 1997; Madsen et al., 2019; Mima and Hallett, 1999; van Elswijk et al., 2010).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Only beta-band rhythm has clear modulatory effects on corticospinal neurons.
source: For instance, there are differences in the cortico-subcortical loops supporting alpha- and beta-band rhythms (Bastos et al., 2014; Leventhal et al., 2012; Schreckenberger et al., 2004; West et al., 2018), and only the latter rhythm has clear modulatory effects on corticospinal neurons (Baker et al., 1997; Madsen et al., 2019; Mima and Hallett, 1999; van Elswijk et al., 2010).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The neurophysiological characteristics of alpha- and beta-band rhythms have often been studied by aggregating these two rhythms into the same (mu-) rhythm category.
source: Yet, the neurophysiological characteristics of alpha- and beta-band rhythms have often been studied by aggregating these two rhythms into the same (mu-) rhythm category (Cuevas et al., 2014; Hari, 2006; Miller et al., 2010), an approach often justified by the partial overlap in their spatial and spectral distributions (Bressler and Richter, 2015; Haegens et al., 2014; Salmelin and Hari, 1994; Szurhaj et al., 2003) and by the temporal correlation of their power envelopes (Carlqvist et al., 2005; de Lange et al., 2008; Tiihonen et al., 1989).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The aggregation of alpha and beta rhythms is often justified by the partial overlap in their spatial and spectral distributions.
source: Yet, the neurophysiological characteristics of alpha- and beta-band rhythms have often been studied by aggregating these two rhythms into the same (mu-) rhythm category (Cuevas et al., 2014; Hari, 2006; Miller et al., 2010), an approach often justified by the partial overlap in their spatial and spectral distributions (Bressler and Richter, 2015; Haegens et al., 2014; Salmelin and Hari, 1994; Szurhaj et al., 2003) and by the temporal correlation of their power envelopes (Carlqvist et al., 2005; de Lange et al., 2008; Tiihonen et al., 1989).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The aggregation of alpha and beta rhythms is often justified by the temporal correlation of their power envelopes.
source: Yet, the neurophysiological characteristics of alpha- and beta-band rhythms have often been studied by aggregating these two rhythms into the same (mu-) rhythm category (Cuevas et al., 2014; Hari, 2006; Miller et al., 2010), an approach often justified by the partial overlap in their spatial and spectral distributions (Bressler and Richter, 2015; Haegens et al., 2014; Salmelin and Hari, 1994; Szurhaj et al., 2003) and by the temporal correlation of their power envelopes (Carlqvist et al., 2005; de Lange et al., 2008; Tiihonen et al., 1989).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: It has been shown that 4–22 Hz activity modulates high-frequency broadband power in primates' frontal cortex.
source: By aggregating those rhythms, it has been recently shown that 4–22 Hz activity modulates high-frequency broadband power in primates' frontal cortex (Bastos et al., 2018; Johnston et al., 2019), and that 10–45 Hz activity is spatially organized in traveling waves (Rubino et al., 2006; Takahashi et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research.

claim: 10–45 Hz activity is spatially organized in traveling waves.
source: By aggregating those rhythms, it has been recently shown that 4–22 Hz activity modulates high-frequency broadband power in primates' frontal cortex (Bastos et al., 2018; Johnston et al., 2019), and that 10–45 Hz activity is spatially organized in traveling waves (Rubino et al., 2006; Takahashi et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The preferred manner in which participants imagined grasping the cylinder depended on the orientation of the cylinder and followed the biomechanical constraints of the body.
source: As seen in Figure 1C, the preferred manner in which participants imagined grasping the cylinder (thumb on black or white part) depended on the orientation of the cylinder and followed the biomechanical constraints of the body.
evidence: Direct observation from behavioral data with reference to figure.

claim: Alpha predominantly supports somatosensory components of a movement.
source: These observations suggest that alpha activity predominantly supports somatosensory components of a movement, in line with its anatomical distribution along the postcentral gyrus.
evidence: Inference drawn from anatomical distribution and stimulation response data.

claim: The temporal dynamics of power changes are highly consistent with previous observations obtained from non-invasive electrophysiological recordings over sensorimotor cortex during performance of the same task.
source: The temporal dynamics of these power changes are highly consistent with previous observations obtained from non-invasive electrophysiological recordings over sensorimotor cortex during performance of the same task (cf. Figure 3 in Brinkman et al., 2014).
evidence: Comparison with prior research findings with citation.

claim: Alpha- and beta-band rhythms involve largely different neuronal ensembles.
source: Furthermore, only 7 out of 30 combined unique electrodes were local maxima for both sensorimotor rhythms, suggesting that alpha- and beta-band rhythms involve largely different neuronal ensembles, χ2(29)=17, p<0.001.
evidence: Inference supported by statistical analysis of electrode overlap.

claim: The neuronal ensembles generating alpha and beta rhythms have no substantial spatiotemporal correspondences, neither within trials nor across trials.
source: These relations between alpha- and beta-band effects indicate that the neuronal ensembles producing these two sensorimotor rhythms have no substantial spatiotemporal correspondences, neither within trials nor across trials.
evidence: Inference drawn from correlation and representational similarity analyses.

claim: The stronger beta-band power reduction in the somatomotor cortex contralateral to the selected arm is associated with a relative disinhibition of somatomotor neuronal populations.
source: Given that both beta-band and 1/f slope indexes were similarly responsive to the laterality of the effector involved in the motor imagery task (Figure 2E), the spatiotemporal correspondence between beta-band rhythm and 1/f slope indicates that the stronger beta-band power reduction in the somatomotor cortex contralateral to the selected arm is associated with a relative disinhibition of somatomotor neuronal populations.
evidence: Inference drawn from correlation between beta power and 1/f slope.

claim: The stronger alpha-band power evoked in the somatosensory cortex ipsilateral to the selected arm is associated with a relative but spatially unspecific inhibition of the sensorimotor cortex.
source: However, there was a significant temporal anti-correlation between local maxima of alpha-band power and 1/f slope (Figure 3A). This observation suggests that the stronger alpha-band power evoked in the somatosensory cortex ipsilateral to the selected arm (Figure 2E) is associated with a relative but spatially unspecific inhibition of the sensorimotor cortex.
evidence: Inference drawn from temporal anti-correlation between alpha power and 1/f slope.

claim: It seems unlikely that the alpha inhibitory effect was driven by somatosensory attention to the hand used during imagery since there were no lateralized power changes in the prestimulus baseline period.
source: It seems unlikely that this alpha inhibitory effect was driven by somatosensory attention to the hand used during imagery since there were no lateralized power changes in the prestimulus baseline period, during which participants knew which hand they would use.
evidence: Inference drawn from absence of baseline power changes.

claim: Beta waves in the motor cortex carry most movement-related information during the preparatory phase of a movement.
source: Speculatively, the spatiotemporal profile of increased excitability observed in the contralateral sensorimotor cortex might support the coordination of multiple sensorimotor cortical ensembles toward a movement-effective neural subspace (Elsayed et al., 2016; Shenoy et al., 2013), possibly implemented as dynamic modulations in direction- and frequency-dependent spatial arrangements of neuron receptor fields (Heitmann et al., 2013). Accordingly, beta waves in the motor cortex carry most movement-related information during the preparatory phase of a movement (Rubino et al., 2006).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Previous micro-ECoG studies in non-human primates have shown systematic phase relationships between motor cortical signals less than a millimeter apart.
source: Previous micro-ECoG studies in non-human primates have shown systematic phase relationships between motor cortical signals less than a millimeter apart (Rubino et al., 2006; Takahashi et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The mean R2 across all slope fits in each individual was 0.95 ± 0.00.
source: Linear fits were used to estimate the steepness of the slope in the 30–50 Hz range (mean R2 across all slope fits in each individual = 0.95 ± 0.00).
evidence: Direct measurement of model fit quality.

claim: The 1/f slope between 30 and 50 Hz best predicts the depth of sleep and anesthesia, more so than slow oscillatory power.
source: Furthermore, recent intracranial recordings in humans find that the slope between 30 and 50 Hz best predicts the depth of sleep and anesthesia, more so than slow oscillatory power (Lendner et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The 1/f slope closely tracks the increase of inhibition induced by propofol across space and time.
source: Notably, electrocorticography recordings in the non-human primate brain indicate that the 1/f slope closely tracks the increase of inhibition induced by propofol across space and time (Gao et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The 1/f slope was sensitive to the laterality of the effector involved in the motor imagery task.
source: Unlike high-frequency activity, the 1/f slope index showed clear functional specificity. This index was sensitive to the laterality of the effector involved in the motor imagery task (Figure 2E).
evidence: Direct observation from data analysis with reference to figure.

claim: The 1/f slope was spatially specific, with a focal reduction of excitation/inhibition ratio at electrodes placed over the central sulcus yielding predominantly somatomotor rather than somatosensory responses (χ2(27)=10.3, p<0.002).
source: This index was also spatially specific, with a focal reduction of excitation/inhibition ratio (i.e., steepest 1/f slopes, indicating stronger local inhibition) at electrodes placed over the central sulcus yielding predominantly somatomotor rather than somatosensory responses following electrical stimulation (χ2(27)=10.3, p<0.002; orange electrodes in Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Statistical analysis of spatial distribution with chi-squared test.

claim: Imagery-related reduction in beta-band power, predominant over the somatomotor cortex contralateral to the selected arm, is associated with a relative disinhibition of somatomotor neuronal populations.
source: These findings suggest that imagery-related reduction in beta-band power, predominant over the somatomotor cortex contralateral to the selected arm, is associated with a relative disinhibition of somatomotor neuronal populations.
evidence: Inference drawn from relationship between beta power and 1/f slope.

claim: Beta-band movement-related disinhibition was embedded within traveling waves moving along a rostro-caudal direction across the fronto-parietal cortex.
source: This beta-band movement-related disinhibition was embedded within traveling waves moving along a rostro-caudal direction across the fronto-parietal cortex.
evidence: Direct observation from traveling wave analysis.

claim: Alpha-band inhibition was embedded within traveling waves along a caudo-rostral direction across the parieto-frontal cortex.
source: This alpha-band inhibition was embedded within traveling waves along a caudo-rostral direction across the parieto-frontal cortex.
evidence: Direct observation from traveling wave analysis.

claim: The evidence points to the relevance of both disinhibition and inhibition mechanisms for precise spatiotemporal coordination of movement-related neuronal populations.
source: We draw two main conclusions from these human neurophysiological observations. First, the evidence points to the relevance of both disinhibition and inhibition mechanisms for precise spatiotemporal coordination of movement-related neuronal populations.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence in the study.

claim: The evidence points to the dramatically different neurophysiological properties of sensorimotor alpha and beta rhythms.
source: Second, the evidence points to the dramatically different neurophysiological properties of sensorimotor alpha and beta rhythms, questioning the practice of aggregating those rhythms when studying cerebral function.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence in the study.

claim: The findings question the practice of aggregating alpha and beta rhythms when studying cerebral function.
source: Second, the evidence points to the dramatically different neurophysiological properties of sensorimotor alpha and beta rhythms, questioning the practice of aggregating those rhythms when studying cerebral function.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Coordinating complex movements requires suppression of task-irrelevant movements and in particular inhibition of their somatosensory correlates.
source: The spatially unspecific inhibition of the ipsilateral sensorimotor cortex suggests that coordinating complex movements also requires suppression of task-irrelevant movements and in particular inhibition of their somatosensory correlates.
evidence: Inference drawn from observed alpha-band effects.

claim: The spatiotemporal profile of increased excitability observed in the contralateral sensorimotor cortex might support the coordination of multiple sensorimotor cortical ensembles toward a movement-effective neural subspace.
source: Speculatively, the spatiotemporal profile of increased excitability observed in the contralateral sensorimotor cortex might support the coordination of multiple sensorimotor cortical ensembles toward a movement-effective neural subspace (Elsayed et al., 2016; Shenoy et al., 2013), possibly implemented as dynamic modulations in direction- and frequency-dependent spatial arrangements of neuron receptor fields (Heitmann et al., 2013).
evidence: Speculative interpretation of findings with citations to theoretical frameworks.

claim: Different cortico-thalamo-cortical and cortico-striatal-thalamo-cortical circuits might lead to different alpha and beta traveling waves across the sensorimotor cortex.
source: Another possibility is that different cortico-thalamo-cortical and cortico-striatal-thalamo-cortical circuits lead to different alpha and beta traveling waves across the sensorimotor cortex (Bastos et al., 2014; Schreckenberger et al., 2004; West et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculative interpretation with citations to prior research.

claim: Ignoring individual differences in spectral distributions and the separation of rhythmic and arrhythmic components led to strong but spurious correlation between alpha and beta power envelopes.
source: Supplementary analyses indicate that ignoring those facts, as standard analytical pipelines do, led to strong but spurious correlation between alpha and beta power envelopes.
evidence: Direct statement about supplementary analysis results.

claim: The spatial separation between alpha- and beta-band cortical sources might prove too subtle for many non-invasive electrophysiological recordings.
source: Furthermore, the spatial separation between alpha- and beta-band cortical sources might prove too subtle for many non-invasive electrophysiological recordings (Brinkman et al., 2014; Fransen et al., 2016).
evidence: Speculative interpretation with citations to prior research.

claim: Statistical power might have been too low for effects based on a subset of trials.
source: This ECoG study involved individuals undergoing presurgical monitoring, a relatively rare clinical procedure with limited opportunities for experimentally controlled observations. The direction of neural effects related to task demand was consistent with the previous observations, yet statistical power might have been too low for effects based on a subset of trials.
evidence: Acknowledgment of study limitation.
